item.title: Five Salvadoran Soldiers Missing in Haiti After Ambush
item.description:
Five Salvadoran soldiers, members of a new U.N.-backed force sent to stop gang violence in Haiti, were ambushed while out shopping near the capital on Sunday and were still missing several hours later, three people familiar with the situation said.

The soldiers were in a vehicle in a gang-controlled area just north of Port-au-Prince when one of the five reported they were under attack and he had been injured. No one has heard from him or the four others in the vehicle since, the people said.

The soldiers were part of the Gang Suppression Force, a U.N.-backed mission aimed at curtailing Haiti’s widespread gang violence. The force is currently made up of fewer than 1,000 personnel from Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia and Sri Lanka.

The Salvadorans operate a helicopter unit that largely handles transportation and other logistics.

It was unclear what the Salvadorans were doing shopping in an area that is considered a restricted “red zone,” which people from the United Nations and diplomatic missions would be prohibited from entering without armored vehicles and weapons.

Other soldiers in the mission were out looking for them, one of the people close to the situation said.

They were shopping in Santo, a community near Croix-de-Bouquets controlled by a gang known as “Chien Méchant,” or “Vicious Dog,” two of the people said. They and the third person all spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the case publicly.

The 400 Mawozo gang, known for conducting widespread kidnappings, also operates in that area.

A spokesman for the Gang Suppression Force declined to confirm any details but said he would release a statement later. A spokesman for the Haitian National Police said he did not have information on the incident.

Residents in the area took to social media to report increased helicopter activity and gunfire.

Haiti is in the throes of an extreme gang crisis which has claimed more than 22,000 lives since 2021. At least 138 people were kidnapped in the first six months of this year, according to U.N. statistics.

The Gang Suppression Force was organized after a previous international mission failed to quell the violence. The new force is supposed to be much larger, made up of 5,500 soldiers from around the world, and with a more robust mandate to operate independently of the police and even make arrests.

In an interview last month, Jack Christofides, special representative of the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti, acknowledged that the force was behind in troop numbers but said the operations were already beginning to chip away at gang activities such as extortion.

“What we’re seeing is that the gangs are starting to attack us, which is a sure sign that we’re affecting their business model, and we’re affecting their revenue collection,” Mr. Christofides said. “But we’ve got a long way to go, we totally recognize that.”

He said the force would have most of its soldiers on the ground by late this year. The violence is so rampant that officials have repeatedly postponed elections, which have not been held in a decade.

André Paultre and Michael Anthony Adams contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump’s Push for Deals With Russia Powers His Frustration With Ukraine
item.description:
He shunted aside a bipartisan law, signed just weeks ago, imposing new tariffs on Russia. He cut a deal to purchase diesel from Moscow. His negotiators agreed on the vague outlines of a deal for much of Lukoil, a battered Russian energy firm. And he called for the replacement of President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, whose success in taking the fight inside Russia deeply frustrates him.

President Trump’s intensifying effort in the past few weeks to rehabilitate Russia and usher President Vladimir V. Putin back into diplomatic society is remarkable for its speed, its characterization of Mr. Zelensky as the primary obstacle to peace, and its brazen denial that Russia is continuing the war that Mr. Trump says he is trying to end.

“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Mr. Trump said on Monday, speaking to reporters outside the White House as he left for a campaign rally. “They haven’t been doing much,” he said, making no mention of the Russian missiles and jet-powered drones that have been targeting apartment buildings in Kyiv and Ukraine’s surviving electricity grid.

In contrast, he said, “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us. Remember that.” He repeated the statement for emphasis. The night before, he wrote on social media that Mr. Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” because it brought him a flow of cash and arms from Europe, making no mention that Ukraine is fighting for its sovereignty and even survival in a war that it did not start.

Mr. Trump’s disdain for Mr. Zelensky is hardly new. Nor is his willingness to give the benefit of the doubt to Mr. Putin, for whom he has often expressed respect and even admiration.

But what is different now is Mr. Trump’s increased determination to force a deal on Mr. Zelensky, telling him that holding out to retain occupied portions of the country’s eastern provinces is not worth it — and that there is money to be made for Ukraine, as well, if it would only drop its objections to an accord, even one written largely on Russia’s terms.

That will be the American message to Mr. Zelensky on Tuesday in Oslo, where Mr. Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, are expected to meet the Ukrainian president.

Participating in the discussion, officials say, will be Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Store, and Alexander Stubb, the president of Finland. (Finland has become an enthusiastic member of the NATO alliance. In World War II, it ceded about 12 percent of its territory to Russia, and has never gotten it back.)

The next day Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner will fly to St. Petersburg, Russia, to meet Mr. Putin in his hometown. There, Mr. Trump’s representatives are expected to take the next step in their efforts to show the benefits of deal-making with Mr. Putin by securing the release of a long-held American.

Mr. Trump discussed the prospect of a hostage release again on Monday, but did not say who was involved. The only American the State Department categorizes as “wrongfully detained” in Russia is Stephen Hubbard, who Russia accused of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine when he was seized in 2022. Mr. Hubbard, who is in his mid-70s, was sentenced to more than six years in a penal colony.

The timing of the release, if it happens, says volumes about Mr. Putin’s strategy. Ridding Russia of an elderly American hostage costs Mr. Putin nothing, and does no good for Ukraine. But in the midst of midterm elections in the United States it allows Mr. Trump to make the case that he is pursuing an America First foreign policy, complete with the heartwarming images of a prisoner being reunited with his family.

But the larger goal here, for Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump, is to normalize a relationship that began to go off the rails more than a decade ago, when Mr. Putin took Crimea, a territory that was integrated with Ukraine during the Soviet era, and when he began to send Russian fighters into eastern Ukraine.

Europe and the United States responded with sanctions. But a year later, then-Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany signed a deal with Mr. Putin to build the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline, calling the Russian leader a “reliable supplier.”

The idea was to reintegrate Russia with the West, in hopes of curbing Mr. Putin’s territorial appetites. The effort failed; seven years later Russia launched its full invasion of Ukraine.

Today, that history, and the rationale behind it, is replaying itself. But it is Mr. Trump who is taking the role that Ms. Merkel once played.

Mr. Trump’s ambitions are clearly bigger. There is already talk of a three-way meeting in China between Mr. Trump, Mr. Putin and Xi Jinping of China on the sidelines of a larger summit of Pacific Rim countries scheduled for next month. Mr. Trump said on Monday the goal would be to discuss the three largest nuclear arsenals in the world, and “denuclearization.” (He likely meant arms control, since none of the three powers seems remotely interested in eliminating their nuclear stockpiles.)

That is exactly what Mr. Putin has in mind: Expanding the discussion with the United States to other topics, apart from Ukraine, that make the long-running conflict look like just one of many issues to be managed. And should the three-way meeting happen, the image of the leaders of the three largest nuclear powers talking would likely carry the suggestion that they are carving the globe into zones of influence, much as Stalin, Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt did at Yalta.

A month later the three are scheduled to be together again, this time at a G20 summit meeting at Mr. Trump’s Doral resort in Florida. Several months ago, Mr. Trump invited Mr. Putin to attend, the first indication that the Russian leader was being called back in from the cold.

To get to that point, however, Mr. Trump had to abandon all talk of helping Ukraine defend a fledgling, if still corruption-plagued, democracy. While he insists that any settlement of the war would come with “security guarantees” to keep Russia from re-invading, Ukrainian officials say they now doubt that the United States would really come to their aid, at least while Mr. Trump is in office.

“The reason it’s hard to think of a precedent of America switching sides in a conflict like this is that there really isn’t one,” said Richard Haass, a longtime diplomat who served Republican and Democratic administrations from the end of the Cold War through the invasion of Iraq 23 years ago.

“What’s unprecedented here is the decision to reverse course and penalize the victim of the invasion — Ukraine — while rewarding the aggressor.”

In fact, as Mr. Haass suggests, there is no satisfying analogy in recent history.

Yes, Nixon shocked allies in 1972 with his opening to China, which led, years later, under President Jimmy Carter, to diplomatic recognition of the People’s Republic, and the withdrawal of formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. But there was no active war when Nixon made the move, and it came with extensive commitments from Washington to protect Taiwan, a strategy that has worked, so far, for nearly half a century.

The United States pulled out of Vietnam, but while it had extensive disputes with South Vietnam it did not openly side with the North. And Mr. Trump, in his first term, and then President Joseph R. Biden Jr., negotiated and executed a deal with the Taliban that quickly led to the takeover of Afghanistan — again, a withdrawal that resulted in the collapse of a government that the United States had tried to prop up. But there have been no business deals brewing with the Taliban leadership.

Mr. Trump’s aides insist that the war between Russia and Ukraine is now at what they call an “inflection point.” The next move is Mr. Zelensky’s, they insist, saying he must prove to Mr. Trump that he, too, is willing to deal with the Russians, even if it means giving up sovereign territory.

That is something the Ukrainian leader once promised to Congress that he would never do. He got a standing ovation in return, and promises that American support would never flag. On Sunday, appearing on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” he acknowledged that the atmosphere was different. Asked if his country could survive without American military and intelligence aid, he responded: “Of course, in all the difficult situations, you have a chance. But we will have a low chance — low chance to survive without support of the United States.”

item.title: Voters in Oil-Rich Alberta Reject Leaving Canada
item.description:
Alberta voted on Monday to remain part of Canada, rejecting a campaign to try to separate the oil-rich western province from the rest of the country.

Voters in a referendum endorsed remaining in Canada over the option of holding a second vote on whether to secede, the public broadcaster CBC News projected late Monday evening local time.

With just over a third of votes counted, 76 percent of voters chose to remain part of Canada with 23 percent seeking another vote.

The referendum reflected the province’s long history of resentment toward the central government, but also more recent discontents. Many of the separatist leaders became politically prominent by organizing large protests against restrictions during the Covid pandemic.

In a brief statement, Danielle Smith, Alberta’s premier, said that “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.”

Thomas Lukaszuk, a former provincial lawmaker whose Forever Canadian organization led the campaign to oppose secession, told supporters that the result “sends a message to the rest of Canada that Alberta will not be the weak link.”

He added, addressing President Trump, who has launched a trade war against Canada and mused about annexing it: “Perhaps most importantly, it will send a very strong message to the rest of the world: Don’t mess with Canada.”

Unlike in Quebec, a province that held two unsuccessful votes on leaving Canada, secessionist sentiments have always been a minority viewpoint in Alberta. Still, before the vote opponents of separatism worried that voters might support holding a second referendum to show their unhappiness with the province’s relationship with Canada, even if they did not want to secede.

Some were also concerned that Albertans loyal to Canada would not turn out to vote out of a belief that the province would never reject the nation.

The vote was the work of Ms. Smith, a conservative who managed to provoke the ire of people on both sides.

Ms. Smith assumed the leadership of the United Conservative Party largely through the support of separatists who were responsible for ousting the previous premier, Jason Kenney, from party leadership.

Supporters of a united Canada were angry at Ms. Smith for adding the question on holding a second referendum on secession to a previously planned referendum with nine other questions. Those questions focused on provincial powers and immigration.

Her move came after a court blocked an attempt by separatists to force a vote to leave Canada through a petition. Federalists said Ms. Smith’s decision was an effort to circumvent the courts and was unconstitutional.

Separatists were dismayed that Ms. Smith created a vote to hold a second vote instead of opting for a clear question on staying in Canada or leaving.

Ms. Smith said that she would vote to remain in Canada. Secession opponents viewed her support for their cause before the vote as anemic, and many of them say they doubt the sincerity of her pledge to remain in Canada.

Last month in an online forum, Ms. Smith, expressed her support for fighting for Alberta within Canada but also laid out what she described as Albertans’ grievances with the federal government.

“When proud, hard-working people feel their contribution is taken for granted,” she said, “and their livelihood is treated as something to be phased out, some begin to ask a painful question: Does this country actually want us?”

She was referring to environmental policies introduced under a former prime minister, Justin Trudeau, that many Albertans considered an effort to shut down their province’s oil sands.

Business groups, former premiers and local politicians were all firmly on the side of remaining in Canada. Economic studies, including one commissioned by the provincial government, forecast that leaving the country would come with enormous costs.

Looming over the vote was Mr. Trump’s rocky relationship with Canada. Some prominent separatists leaders traveled to Washington three times last year seeking support from the Trump administration at meetings with low-level State Department officials.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, who was raised in Edmonton, the provincial capital, called the referendum a “dangerous bluff.” Mr. Carney was governor of the Bank of England when Britain voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

“Is it helpful to ask these fundamental questions?” he asked in May after Ms. Smith’s announcement of the referendum. “No, it’s not helpful. Of course it’s not. Is it the democratic will of Albertans? Did they vote for this in the last provincial election? No, they didn’t.”

Mr. Carney received an enthusiastic reception at two large rallies for those supporting remaining in Canada last week in Edmonton and Calgary. Ms. Smith did not attend either event.

Many separatist leaders are veterans of the large protests in Alberta during the Covid pandemic that were aimed at public health restrictions. They never laid out specific plans for a independent Alberta and their various factions offered a variety of futures, including a state guided by Christian doctrine. Many of their complaints about Canada are based on economic issues.

About 1.3 million people, just over a third of all eligible voters, cast ballots by mail or during early voting. Because voters had to mark 10 separate paper ballots and then place them into an equal number of ballot boxes, there were long lines at many of the 1,400 polling stations on Monday.

Before the vote, some leaders of the separatist movements suggested that they might not accept the results.

Mitch Sylvestre, a prominent separatist leader, said in an interview last Thursday that he was concerned about potential irregularities in voting. He also questioned the validity of many mail-in ballots.

“I’m not going to stand on a pedestal and start screaming and yelling ‘election interference’ until there’s real good evidence that it happened,” Mr. Sylvestre said. “All I’m saying is I’m very skeptical, as are a lot, or most of, our people.”

item.title: 14 Dead After Gold Mine Collapses in Colombia
item.description:
A gold mine operating without permits collapsed on Monday morning in Colombia, killing 14 people and injuring seven others, the authorities said.

The collapsed mine was in Santa Bárbara de Iscuandé, a remote town in Colombia’s southwestern Nariño region. The governor’s office confirmed the deaths in a statement, and Gov. Luis Alfonso Escobar said the search and rescue operation had been called off.

It was unclear who owned the mine, or how many people were inside when it collapsed.

In August, another mine collapsed in Policarpa, a town in Nariño about 65 miles southeast of Santa Barbara, killing 13 people and injuring four others, according to local media.

Small-scale mining operations have sprung up in Colombia, fueled by the rising global price of gold, which surpassed $5,000 an ounce this year. Many are unlicensed, and some are controlled by criminals, cartels and armed rebel groups. A New York Times investigation found that the United States Mint had bought gold that originated from a mine in the country’s northwest operated by a Colombian drug cartel under Treasury Department sanctions.

In a statement on Monday, the Colombian ombudsman’s office called for armed groups around Nariño to guarantee safe access for emergency workers and humanitarian aid to reach Santa Bárbara.

The authorities in Nariño did not specify the victims’ ages or genders.

“There are entire families who have lost their lives in this regrettable event, which fills us with great sorrow,” Mr. Escobar said.

item.title: The British Police Rearrest Two in Connection With Alleged Terror Plot
item.description:
The British counterterrorism police rearrested two men on Tuesday in connection with an alleged terror plot at a British air base last month and said for the first time that they believe the men were working on behalf of Iran.

The two men from London, a 24-year-old British national and a 25-year-old dual British and Iranian national, had been released on bail after their initial arrests on suspicion of planning to carry out a terrorist attack at R.A.F. Fairford, a base in England used by American bombers.

In a statement on Tuesday, the police said the men had been taken back into custody on suspicion of “assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act.” The statement said that “the country to which the investigation relates is Iran.”

The British police had not publicly said that they believed Iran was involved in the incident at the base, though Prime Minister Andy Burnham said as much late last month.

“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at R.A.F. Fairford,” Mr. Burnham told the BBC in an interview on Sept. 30.

Details of the threat against the air base remain hazy nearly a month after police responded to a telephone call alerting them to three white vans headed toward Fairford. Police later said the call had come from one of the men inside the vans but have not explained why the man decided to call the authorities.

The arrests of five men on the morning of Sept. 27 triggered more than two days of anxiety as the police and military used a bomb disposal robot to examine the vans. More than 85 nearby homes were evacuated.

Within two days, all five men had been released on bail after the bomb units failed to discover any explosives in the vans. Two more men were arrested soon after, and they, too, were released on bail. None of the men have been charged with a crime.

Early this month, the United States abruptly flew all of its bombers out of Fairford and returned them to bases in the United States. The withdrawal happened so quickly that some of the planes and their flight crews left while aerial refueling aircraft were still being scrambled to support them.

Two U.S. officials said at the time that commanders had received new threats of an Iran-backed plot against the installation.

item.title: Is Putin’s Waiting Game Working?
item.description:
Donald Trump not only wants to buy diesel from Vladimir Putin — he’s suggesting Europeans start buying energy again from Russia, too. It’s a stunning reversal: Just a few years ago, major European countries like Germany were dangerously dependent on Moscow for cheap energy. It was the United States that called out that dependence.

Europe’s governments, some of them deeply unpopular, were predictably dismayed by Trump’s recent comments. But the continent’s ascendant and Russia-friendly far right cheered. Today I write about why this might be less a story about a surprise reversal of U.S. strategy and more one about Putin’s long-term strategy paying off.

For years, the war in Ukraine has effectively been a stalemate. The front has moved at a crawl, and at an appalling cost.

Western countries remained more or less united in supporting Ukraine against Russia, until Trump returned to office early last year. Since then, American military and financial aid to Ukraine has fallen sharply, shifting much of the burden to Europe.

Now, another turning point may be at hand.

Over the weekend, following his decision to waive some U.S. sanctions and buy Russian diesel, Trump went a step further. As my colleagues report, he has proposed that European countries resume buying Russian natural gas.

That idea has been categorically ruled out in many corners of Europe. But not in all of them. Alice Weidel, a leader of the far-right AfD party, told the German Parliament last week that sanctions on Russia were “ruining our own economy.” Marine Le Pen, the leader of France’s far right, criticized the European Union for leading “an energy war against Russia, when we haven’t got any energy.”

Putin has long believed that his commitment to waging war on Ukraine would outlast the commitment of Western allies to defending Ukraine.

It’s cost him more than a million troops killed or wounded, and counting. But his strategy might finally be paying off.

Putin’s waiting game

When Putin launched the full invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he expected it to be a quick war. One reason that didn’t happen was the resolve and unity of Ukrainians to put up a fight. Another was the resolve and unity of Western allies to help.

I spoke with my colleague Anton Troianovski, who covered the invasion as Moscow bureau chief and is now our global affairs correspondent. Anton told me that Putin was taken by surprise that Western countries managed to construct a united front.

That meant not only supplying Ukraine with weapons, money and intelligence. It also meant weaning European countries off cheap Russian gas at a major economic cost to Moscow, but to Europe as well. Germany, the continent’s biggest economy, relied on Russia for more than half the gas it used before the invasion; it now pays more for gas from other countries.

The resulting rise in energy costs, and its economic and political fallout in Western countries, have been at the core of Putin’s strategy to drag the war out, Anton said.

“It’s taking far longer than Putin anticipated,” Anton told me. “But he’s always been convinced that it’s only a matter of time until Western unity on Ukraine splinters.”

That explains why Putin has refused to end the war, time and time again, even as Trump has gone out of his way to offer him concessions.

On the campaign trail, Trump boasted that he could end the war within 24 hours. Three weeks after returning to the White House, he had his first phone call with Putin, followed by more promises of ending the war.

Six months later, Trump gave Putin the red carpet treatment in Alaska and said a cease-fire deal was close.

Then in November, Trump promoted a 28-point peace plan widely seen as favorable to Russia, again promising to end the war.

This shows two things, Anton told me: how far Putin is prepared to mortgage his own country to keep fighting this war in pursuit of his core demands — annexing territory, disarming Ukraine and ruling out any NATO involvement there. And how far Trump is prepared to go to give him what he wants.

The West’s pivot?

Putin has already gotten some of what he wants. Trump is buying Russian diesel, he’s getting even tougher on Ukraine and he’s leaning on Europe to buy Russian gas.

At the same time, many European governments are becoming weaker as populist parties friendlier to Russia are getting stronger (aided by Russian disinformation campaigns aimed at eroding trust in Western governments).

In France, Le Pen is the front-runner in presidential elections next year. In Germany, the pro-Russia AfD is now the most popular party. The rise of far-right parties in Europe has its own homegrown dynamic. But, as Anton put it, “it clearly dovetails with Putin’s efforts to splinter the Western coalition.”

In Washington, the splintering seems far advanced. Trump blames Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, for the ongoing war (Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he posted on social media Sunday) and shrugs off Russian bombardments that are causing sharply higher civilian casualties (“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” he said Monday).

The language matters. It points to Trump’s increased determination to force a deal on Zelensky, my colleague David Sanger wrote, “even one written largely on Russia’s terms.”

Which would be the greatest vindication of all for Putin’s strategy.

The latest: More than a week into his war of words with Trump, Zelensky met in Oslo yesterday with Steve Witkoff, Trump’s envoy.

France extended curfews in parts of Paris and other cities for a second night following weekend riots. But the government is in no position to use money to bring calm to the streets. That’s because it’s also fighting a potential crisis in its bond market.

The British police rearrested two men in connection with an alleged terror plot at a British air base and said that they believed the men were working on behalf of Iran.

Residents of Alberta voted overwhelmingly to remain part of Canada. Prime Minister Mark Carney called it “a great result for Canada.”

Britain will send fighter jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from missile and drone attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.

Officials in Taiz, one of Yemen’s largest cities, warned of a humanitarian disaster as a Houthi siege of the city entered its third week.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in India for meetings with business executives including Asia’s two richest men, Gautam Adani and Mukesh Ambani.

Trump is on the campaign trail ahead of the midterms, talking up his record even as political turmoil engulfs Washington. Tyler Page, one of our White House correspondents, explains in the video below.

Global philanthropic organizations are in a race for dollars from A.I. fortunes that could bring a monumental wave of new funding for health aid.

A plan to build one of Europe’s largest data centers on a patch of farmland in Devon, southwest England, has run into strong opposition from residents, who quickly organized to oppose the project.

Banners protesting the “Devon data monster” hang in shop windows, and it’s hard to find anyone with a positive word for the project. Yet the data center also promises a surge of investment in Britain’s sputtering economy. Read more about the data center backlash.

The fox collie has roots in the Scottish Highlands. It can work a ranch and run all day, but it can also play fetch, hang out on long car rides and relax next to you in bed. Unlike Border collies, which seem unable to sit still, fox collies are pros at the art of chill.

The fox collie is not a widely known breed, but Andy DuVigneaud, a winemaker in California, is out to change that. He sees the dog as the ideal pet for lonely and flailing humans in 2026. Read more to meet DuVigneaud and some very nice dogs.

item.title: China Condemns U.S. Ban on DeepSeek A.I. in Government Systems
item.description:
China on Tuesday accused the United States of discrimination “under the pretext of so-called national security” after a U.S. order banned products by the Chinese artificial intelligence giant DeepSeek from the technological systems of many U.S. government agencies.

The American order, published on Monday but issued in July, and the Chinese recriminations inflamed tensions between the two nations amid their frenzied race for A.I. primacy. Some experts have likened the close competition to the nuclear arms race of the 20th century, with potentially huge stakes for humanity.

Citing fears that China may gain access to sensitive U.S. data from DeepSeek to “produce actionable intelligence,” the Department of Homeland Security ordered the removal of all the company’s products — and those from other firms reliant on its open-source offerings — from the informational technology systems in civilian executive branch agencies. It also banned future acquisitions of the products.

In issuing the order, which went into effect this summer, U.S. officials contended that the China’s legal system allows that government extensive access to Chinese company infrastructure, making the U.S. government vulnerable to the exposure of sensitive information. The assertion angered Chinese officials, who on Tuesday accused the United States of using disingenuous national security concerns to suppress Chinese companies.

China’s Ministry of Commerce said in a statement that China had passed laws to protect cybersecurity and data privacy to ensure that its companies can comply with relevant laws worldwide. It called on the United States to “withdraw” any restrictive measures.

“China has consistently opposed the overgeneralization of the concept of national security and the politicization of science, technology and trade issues,” Mao Ning, a spokeswoman for China’s foreign ministry, said at a briefing on Tuesday. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises.”

DeepSeek stunned the world last year when it announced that it had built one of the most powerful A.I. systems with far fewer computer chips than many thought necessary, and at a remarkably low training cost of less than $6 million.

U.S. agencies accused DeepSeek last month of being “misleading,” saying that figure did not reflect “the true cost” of data acquired maliciously. The accusations echoed those made by major American A.I. companies like Anthropic and OpenAI.

China’s Commerce Ministry called those claims groundless, and part of a U.S. effort to monopolize the A.I. industry. It vowed that “China will take resolute countermeasures” if Chinese companies are suppressed or restricted as a result.

The Chinese government rejected accusations by the F.B.I. and other agencies that DeepSeek and other major Chinese A.I. companies engaged in “aggressive, malicious and targeted” industrial-scale copying of frontier A.I. models developed in the United States “in an attempt to bridge the technological and performance gaps,” most “likely” with their government’s awareness.

Last week, China’s Commerce Ministry and its Ministry of Science and Technology proposed new export and licensing controls on some A.I. technologies to protect its domestic industry, mirroring the American approach. While the Chinese proposal has not been finalized and excludes open-source models that have already been released, the newly listed technologies now face registration requirements.

Tensions between the two countries are growing at a time when some say that coordination is tantamount to the A.I. race.

The United States has in recent years restricted the exports of advanced computer chips to limit China’s A.I. development. DeepSeek and other Chinese companies have raced forward despite the limits. And this past spring, DeepSeek said its new model relied on chips made by the Chinese tech giant Huawei, a milestone in China’s effort to reduce the need for foreign technology.

DeepSeek is among several prominent Chinese companies, like Moonshot AI and Alibaba, that allow developers to download open-source systems free and build products with them, unlike OpenAI and Anthropic, which can charge fees.

That has made Chinese A.I. appealing to American businesses, giving them access to models deemed nearly as effective by many experts at a much lower cost and potentially raising challenges for Anthropic and OpenAI ahead of planned initial public offerings.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The companies have denied the suit’s claims.).

It is not clear how reliant U.S. agencies have been on DeepSeek or on products that integrate its technology. The Homeland Security order gave no specifics, and when reached for comment, the department did not answer questions about the extent to which the targeted products had been integrated.

In a statement to The Times on Tuesday, a spokesperson for the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said that new exclusion and removal orders addressing DeepSeek were issued on Friday by the heads of the Department of Defense, Homeland Security and the National Intelligence Program requiring agencies to identify and remove DeepSeek and affiliated products.

DeepSeek could not be reached by phone on Monday, and it did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

The Homeland Security Department is not the first federal or state agency to restrict or ban the use of DeepSeek in its official systems or devices.

The Commerce Department, the Navy, the Defense Information Systems Agency and NASA have all barred its use, and states including Texas, New York and Virginia have prohibited the use of DeepSeek products in government work.

Other countries have made similar moves. Among them, France and Australia last year blocked the use of DeepSeek tech from all government systems. Italy also banned its products from app stores, citing concerns about data protection.

Xinyun Wu contributed reporting.

item.title: Nigeria Announces First Case of Ebola in Current Outbreak
item.description:
Nigeria on Tuesday announced its first case of Ebola during the current outbreak, as the virus continued to spread internationally.

The woman who was infected recently flew to Nigeria from Uganda and received the diagnosis several days after starting treatment at a private hospital in Nigeria’s capital, Abuja, according to a statement by the Nigerian health ministry.

“She is currently in isolation and receiving medical care,” said the statement, which was posted on social media.

The epicenter of the world’s fastest growing Ebola outbreak is at the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, more than 1,600 miles southeast of Abuja. More than 4,600 people have died in Congo since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, according to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the continent’s main public health body.

The disease has also spread to across Congo’s borders to neighboring Uganda, where it was quickly contained after just 20 cases and three deaths, and then this month to Kenya.

The authorities in Kenya said Tuesday that a ninth person had tested positive for the virus since Oct. 6, when Ebola was found in a Kenyan man who had arrived from Congo via a flight from Uganda. He subsequently died. They said that everyone who tested positive for the disease had already been in quarantine.

The announcement of the case in Nigeria will probably concern the public, but medical experts say that single cases are relatively easy to contain as long as the correct health measures are followed. These include prompt isolation of the patient to prevent further contamination, particularly of medical staff, and the identification of the people with whom the patient came into contact.

In all, 44 contacts of the female patient, who was not named, have been identified, the health ministry said. Ebola can be spread only after an infected person develops symptoms, so the vast majority of people who are quarantined because of potential exposure do not have the virus.

However, the fact that the woman had been treated for several days before her diagnosis suggested that health care workers, and possibly others, may have been exposed.

The international health authorities have been quick to defend Nigeria, praising its prompt announcement of the virus, in line with a policy that encourages governments to be transparent about Ebola.

“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” said Dr. Jean Kaseya, director general of Africa C.D.C., on social media. He called it “an extremely serious threat,” given that nearly half of all people who contract the virus die. Bundibugyo is the strain of Ebola in the current outbreak.

Early in the outbreak, an American doctor involved in Ebola care in Congo was evacuated to Germany after testing positive. He recovered. France recorded a case in June, when a French doctor also treating patients in Congo returned home. He has since recovered. A health worker involved in the response was also medically evacuated to the Netherlands this month after testing positive.

During the epidemic that started in 2014 in West Africa — the worst the world has seen in terms of the number of deaths — a few Ebola cases spread to Nigeria. But the Nigeria outbreak was then swiftly contained, in part because of the quick reactions and courage of doctors who have since been lauded as national heroes.

item.title: Lavish Art Basel Paris Preview Draws Interest Under Shadow of Protests
item.description:
It’s an art world golden ticket. The annual invitation to mix and mingle for hours in a magnificent venue with the planet’s wealthiest collectors at the Avant-Première preview of the Art Basel Paris fair.

But Tuesday’s ultra exclusive private viewing in the Belle Époque splendor of the Grand Palais was at risk of losing its appeal for international visitors. Protests, riots and looting have been gathering momentum across Paris and other French cities recently, prompting the authorities to impose curfews this week at some flash points.

The violence is the culmination of weeks of mostly peaceful anti-government protests across France, set off by students aggrieved by the conditions at their high schools. The numbers swelled as the protesters were joined by other disaffected groups upset about the rising cost of living and other grievances, as well as some bent on causing criminal damage.

By Monday, the violence had largely abated, though the scent of burned out cars, shops and electric bikes still lingered faintly in the drizzly Paris air. Still, art students showed their solidarity by blocking the entrance to the Louvre museum, forcing it to shut down.

And on Tuesday, the Avant-Première preview went on as planned with a healthy turnout.

For days leading up to the event, international collectors were on their smartphones seeking reassurance that it was safe to travel to Paris. On Sunday, Art Basel reassured invitees that the Grand Palais was surrounded by anti-ram barriers and 24-hour security patrols.

“The pictures of the riots were so scary,” said Saloni Doshi, an Indian collector of contemporary art based in Mumbai, who was one of the early arrivals at Avant-Première. “My collector friends asked me if it was safe to come on this trip. I had to say ‘yes’ to at least three of them.”

Art Basel Paris this year features 211 international dealers, each of whom is allocated six “plus one” Avant-Première invitations for prized clients. It has become Europe’s pre-eminent fair devoted to high-value modern and contemporary artworks.

The event is a particular favorite with wealthy American collectors and their advisers, lured by the glamour of the Grand Palais and by the quality of the French capital’s public and private museums, hotels, restaurants and shops.

As a result, Art Basel exhibitors bring their most valuable works to the Paris edition.

Last year, two paintings sold for more than $20 million each. This year, Pace Di Donna Schrader Galleries of New York brought the rare Amedeo Modigliani painting of a nude, “Nu Étendu (Lolotte)” from 1917, priced at more than $100 million.

“The media have blown this out of all proportion,” the New York-based exhibitor Fergus McCaffrey said of the jitters over civil unrest. “Headlines like ‘France in Flames’ were a complete misrepresentation,” he added, saying that he had seen the key American clients he had expected. “Everyone came.”

As Avant-Première closed at 7 p.m. and visitors headed out for dinner, Jon Shirley and Kim Richter, Komal Shah, Don and Mera Rubell, Pamela Joyner, Marguerite Hoffman and Glenn Fuhrman emerged among the major American private collectors spotted at the preview.

Nonetheless, the Paris preview seemed less frenetic and less dominated by Americans than the last conclave of top collectors in this city in 2025.

“Saturday wasn’t fun,” the New York art adviser Candace Worth said at the preview. “I had tear gas going off under my window,” she added, recalling disturbances near her hotel over the weekend. “I was speaking to Americans online before the fair. I wasn’t aware that any of them canceled, but that doesn’t mean they didn’t.”

item.title: As Alberta Rejects Separatism, Carney Gets Much of the Credit
item.description:
For Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, the decision by oil-rich Alberta to ask voters whether to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on secession came, as he put it last week, “at the worst possible time.”

But timing aside, Monday’s resounding vote to keep the western province within Canada both strengthens national unity and eliminates a significant distraction as Mr. Carney works to form new global alliances in the face of the trade and diplomatic war that President Trump has waged against Canada since he returned to office.

After months of campaigning, 75.2 percent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada, while 24.8 percent favored holding a second, binding vote on separation, according to unofficial results.

Neither Mr. Carney nor his Liberal government had a formal role in the referendum, which was called by Danielle Smith, Alberta’s conservative premier. But many analysts attributed the strong vote for Canada to policies Mr. Carney, who was raised in the province, introduced over the past year and to his campaigning for continued unity here.

“Carney was huge,” said Duane Bratt, a professor at Mount Royal University in Calgary, Alberta, who studies Alberta politics. “His working with Smith really took the wind out of separatism, and that’s why the separatists were just flailing.”

He added, “Mark Carney is the most popular politician in the province right now.”

Even after accounting for Mr. Carney’s upbringing in Edmonton, for a Liberal prime minister to enjoy outsize popularity is an anomaly in Alberta, the home of Canadian conservatism, where Conservative candidates frequently win federal elections in landslides.

Even today, many Albertans still complain about a government policy almost 50 years ago under the Liberal prime minister Pierre Elliot Trudeau. His short-lived National Energy Program of 1980, which sought to lower the Canadian price for oil, was popular elsewhere in Canada. But it was deeply resented in Alberta, where it was widely seen as an intrusion on the provinces’ control over natural resources.

When Mr. Carney, former governor of the central banks of Canada and of England, entered politics last year, Ms. Smith seized every opportunity to criticize what she called the federal government’s “nine bad laws,” environmental measures introduced by his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, Pierre’s son. She also relentlessly pushed for a second oil pipeline to the Pacific Coast from her landlocked province.

Since then, Mr. Carney has replaced most of the “nine bad laws” with what he calls “cooperative federalism.” The new approach includes a new system that he said would speed up environmental and regulatory approvals of large projects, including oil and gas developments. More significantly, he said the federal government would build and largely finance an oil pipeline to a new ship terminal near Vancouver, British Columbia, the province just west of Alberta.

While Mr. Carney’s changes were condemned by some environmentalists and Indigenous communities, they undercut separatist claims that Canada holds Alberta back from its full economic potential.

As a result, Mr. Bratt said, separatist campaigners were reduced to saying that Mr. Carney “was going to cancel the pipeline the day after the referendum or ask why he wasn’t building it personally by hand — just all sorts of crazy stuff.”

Polls show that Albertans support Mr. Carney’s defiant approach to Mr. Trump, as do Canadians generally. Ms. Smith, by contrast, who became leader of the United Conservative Party and then premier largely with the support of separatists, has frequently urged caution and restraint in dealing with Washington.

She initially joined other provinces’ leaders in banning the sale of American beer, wine and spirits from the provincial liquor distribution system to pressure the Trump administration. But she soon allowed the products’ return, leaving Alberta as the only province without any measures against American alcohol.

Ms. Smith and Mr. Carney also contrasted during the referendum campaign. After a court quashed separatist efforts to force a direct question on leaving through a petition, Ms. Smith changed the law to add the separatism question to a previously planned referendum. She then alienated separatists by saying that she would vote for Canada; she did not require her party’s elected members to follow suit. Her own campaigning for Canada was limited, and she often focused on reasons for leaving the country.

Although Mr. Carney acknowledged that Albertans have causes for complaint and that Canada “isn’t perfect,” he vigorously pushed back against the separatist movement and the referendum. His message was well received. About 7,000 people lined up last week in Calgary, the province’s largest city — some for up to two hours — for a rally where he was the headliner.

On Tuesday, Mr. Carney made no attempt to hide his delight as he headed into a cabinet meeting in Ottawa.

“It’s a great result for Canada, thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity,” he told reporters, adding in French: “It’s a good day for Canada.”

item.title: ‘People Are So Rude’: Can Britain Shhhh Headphone Dodgers on Trains?
item.description:
Many Londoners would agree that there is a set of unwritten rules for travelers on the city’s Underground and iconic red buses. Eye contact is largely a no-go. Interactions are kept at a minimum, with exceptions for cute babies and dogs.

But in recent years, one long-held convention, that riders should keep their electronic devices quiet, has appeared to be crumbling — in many places around the world — as some travelers scroll videos or play music without headphones.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain this week announced a national campaign against what he described as “one of the most annoying things on public transport.”

The government is urging passengers to use headphones on trains or risk being asked to leave the train or face a fine, and is publicizing existing policies that allow the local authorities to issue fines of up to 100 pounds (about $134) to tackle loud music on buses. The reality of how that will be enforced remains unclear, however.

On Tuesday morning, London commuters weighed in on the plans.

Patricia Foley has lived in London her whole life and said that she always felt that people using public transportation were polite. In recent years, though, she feels that has changed.

“People are so rude now, and I am not sure why,” she said. “And I would never challenge anyone myself.”

She said she was happy about government efforts to address antisocial behavior, as it would take the responsibility off other passengers.

“I think it’s a brilliant proposal because who wants to sit next to someone watching a film or something loud?” she said. “But how do you implement it? They are not going to spend money on people patrolling this.”

Geoff Newnham said that he found music blaring from people’s phones irritating and that he was in favor of the idea of fines “because it gets the message out there.” But he, too, was skeptical it could work.

“I think the reality is that enforcing those fines is going to be very difficult, and it’s probably just going to cause more issues,” he said. “The people that are quite happy to obnoxiously play their music are not going to be the people who will necessarily respond well to being challenged over it.”

He and his partner, Freya Skerten, had spent a long weekend in London with their 11-week-old baby and were waiting to board a train home. Ms. Skerten gently rocked their daughter’s stroller back and forth in an effort to keep her asleep as she explained that most people kept to themselves on public transportation.

“I think it’s a real British thing, isn’t it?” she said, but added with a smile, “Unless you have a baby — then everyone wants to speak to you.”

Ken Oluwadare was quietly scrolling through his phone on his way to university. He is studying for a degree in popular music performance.

“I’m studying drumming and I love music, but it’s only on when I am wearing my headphones,” he said.

In a hushed voice, he said he would prefer to see a campaign for more public awareness rather than fines. “Maybe the way they announce the next stop, they should also be telling people, ‘On this train, we won’t be allowing any loud noises.’”

“I don’t think it’s going to be effective; it’s nonsense,” Emma Hawkins said of the government’s plans. “I’d rather they spend more time dealing with other crime.”

She and her daughter, Bea Hawkins, were waiting for a train in Paddington Station and agreed that noisy neighbors on the bus and train were a real nuisance.

“I think it’s long overdue for someone to do something about this,” Bea said. “Especially when someone is watching Reels, it’s so annoying because it’s this different blast of music every few seconds,” she added, referring to Instagram’s short-form vertical videos.

Tosh Polpitiye, who was waiting on the train platform with his two dogs, Guinness and Ouzo, during the Tuesday rush hour, said he thought fines could have a positive effect on riders’ experience.

“I don’t want to hear other people’s phones,” he said. “I don’t want to hear what they are listening to. I don’t even like it when they have their speakers on to make a call.” He added, “You aren’t in your house.”

The fines could make more people compliant, he said, likening it to penalties for breaking the speed limit: “It’s consequences that typically make people not want to do those actions.”

item.title: Modi Seeks to Calm Allies by Shackling Gen Z Protests
item.description:
The ongoing youth protests rocking India caught Prime Minister Narendra Modi by surprise when they first broke out in the summer.

His deployment of police batons and tear gas, plus social media videos seeking to connect with Gen Z in their style, did little to contain them. A rare political climb-down, by sacrificing his education minister, got the protesters to go home for the time being, but it also emboldened his opponents.

So when the protesters announced another demonstration in the capital earlier this month, this time angry over changes to the nation’s voter roll, many leaders of the strongman’s own governing coalition were alarmed, as Mr. Modi maintained his trademark silence on anything negative.

But how Mr. Modi has dealt with the unrest in recent days — locking down the heart of New Delhi, detaining protest leaders and rounding up protesters by the thousands — signaled a better prepared strategy that has reassured some of his backers that he can stall the momentum of the protest movement, according to interviews with more than half a dozen senior members of the governing coalition. Most of them asked not be identified as they are not authorized to publicly discuss internal strategy.

The government’s approach is two-pronged, they said.

First: Quash any mobilizing effort that suggests that public anger is the continuation of the organic Gen Z eruption over the summer that, by all accounts, unsettled Mr. Modi’s grip on power.

Second: Allow the gatherings of the traditional opposition parties to go ahead, framing the fight squarely against a traditional foe that Mr. Modi has repeatedly beaten at elections and is confident of vanquishing again.

For now, the approach appears to be working.

The “cockroach” youth movement — which began this summer over the failings of the education system and was revived this autumn over accusations that Mr. Modi is manipulating India’s election system — has become bogged down by the enormous powers of the state thrown at them.

Their momentum has deflated as their leaders move in and out of detention, and get tangled up in legal cases that could follow them for years. Security forces have met protest calls by putting locations under lockdown and flooding the area with uniformed officers. Organizers and supporters are stopped at the city gates, pulled out of trains and buses, and in many cases held in their homes or barricaded inside their university campuses.

Broadcast media seen as friendly to the government has then declared the low turnout a flop.

The organized political opposition, on the other hand, has received a boost from the rare public challenge to Mr. Modi. But the anti-Modi coalition has long been a fragile one, its unity frequently tested by internal competition on local turf across the country.

Mr. Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party has long portrayed the strongman as less of a prime minister of a coalition government, and more of an executive ruler. It is framing the current agitation as an effort by Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition bloc, to topple Mr. Modi through violent means.

“Their intention is pure and simple regime change,” Smriti Irani, a senior B.J.P. leader and former cabinet minister who defeated Mr. Gandhi in his constituency in 2019, said in TV appearances last week. “An unelectable prince, who hopes to be emperor one day, is now throwing a political tantrum.”

Still, Mr. Modi has found himself in troubled waters that he has not experienced in his 12 years at the national helm, many of the governing coalition leaders said. A nonpartisan civil society is managing to break through and question government failures in ways that the B.J.P. cannot easily dismiss as old-school partisan politics.

There was already some discontent within Mr. Modi’s camp before the protest movement. Some figures within the B.J.P. and other parties in his coalition had become disgruntled by how much power has become centralized.

“The opposition is not a problem for them,” said Durga Nand Jha, an academic who leads a think tank affiliated with the B.J.P.’s parent organization. “The problem is, why is the public and their own supporters not defending them? They are struggling to consolidate their own supporters in this moment — some are opposing, some are silent, some are just sitting at home.”

The B.J.P. has become overly dependent on state levers and electoral machinations at the cost of political dynamism, according to party leaders and analysts. In several states, supporters have been disheartened over what they see as a heavily top-down approach to local elections and issues.

Party leaders, however, expressed confidence that they would still be better placed than the opposition Congress Party, which is struggling to translate the growing popularity of its leader, Mr. Gandhi, to an actual revival of its cadres at the local and state levels.

“A few thousand protesters here and there — students, farmers, businessmen — don’t make a dent in our winnibility,” said Krishna Kant Shukla, a B.J.P. leader in Uttar Pradesh, India’s largest state of 240 million people, which will hold an election next year.

The summer youth protests had drawn large crowds, including many youth from families not associated with the opposition, according to one B.J.P. leader and two leaders of parties in the ruling coalition. The youth were irreverent in how they poked fun at Mr. Modi with their placards and memes. Many, on camera, suggested they came from families who supported the ruling party.

The task of handling political agitation falls to Amit Shah, Mr. Modi’s powerful home minister, who is his effective No. 2 and has been at his side for over two decades.

Ahead of the protests this month in New Delhi, Mr. Shah deployed tens of thousands of security forces and barricaded a large swath of the city center to make sure crowds similar to those from the summer could not gather.

But even during the crackdown, there was an interesting let up: The police allowed a large gathering of the Congress Party and its opposition alliance partners to crowd into central Delhi. Mr. Modi’s supporters then cast the gathering as Mr. Gandhi attempting a power grab — choosing a preferred foe to address rather than acknowledging that it was facing a problem with youth anger.

Behind the bravado, Mr. Modi’s party is facing the moment on shakier ground.

After losing his party’s parliamentary majority in 2024, Mr. Modi has been dependent on several coalition partners.

How he holds together his alliance will be key, particularly if the youth movement grows and his partners see their ties with the ruling party as a liability.

Leaders from two parties that have brought support to Mr. Modi complained that Mr. Modi and Mr. Shah rarely consult leaders of their own B.J.P., let alone those from coalition partners. A leader from one of the allied parties likened Mr. Modi to Indira Gandhi, the prime minister who suspended democracy for two years in the 1970s. Neither could take criticism, the party leader said.

As the youth movement has faced the brunt of the state’s suppression, its leaders have been questioned for not coordinating more closely with the organized opposition to find safety in numbers.

But Anish Gawande, a spokesman for an opposition party who also maintains close ties to leaders of the youth movement, said that such merging would play right into Mr. Modi’s designs.

“It’s only if the third space opens up that the opposition can revive itself,” Mr. Gawande said.

He said the youth movement needed to reinvent itself in the face of government suppression, but the harsh crackdown was helping with the movement’s broader mission for accountability: by exposing the repressive measures of Mr. Modi’s government. Its heavy-handedness, particularly the repeated detention of youth leaders for nonviolent marches, may backfire with a younger generation.

“You have to realize that you cannot constantly do this, that these security forces cannot sit in Delhi for the next year,” Mr. Gawande said. “So just as the state tires us out, we also tire the state out.”

item.title: Hegseth Said to Make Unannounced Visit to Israel for Talks With Netanyahu
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, according to two people briefed on the meeting.

Mr. Hegseth made his trip a day after President Trump publicly endorsed Mr. Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political survival in a tough election campaign.

The Trump administration has expressed growing frustration in recent weeks as diplomatic efforts have failed to produce a lasting deal to end the war on Iran, and Mr. Trump has threatened to launch new strikes.

Mr. Hegseth also met with Israel Katz, Israel’s defense minister, said the two people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private meetings.

The details of the conversations between Mr. Hegseth and his Israeli counterparts were not immediately clear. Mr. Netanyahu’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Hegseth’s trip to Israel and his meeting with Mr. Netanyahu was first reported by the news outlet Axios.

In late September, Mr. Trump suggested at the United Nations General Assembly that Washington could pursue renewed military action, and he threatened to “annihilate” Iran. This month, Mr. Trump said on social media that he would not launch a new attack before the midterm elections in November.

On Sunday, in a post thanking Mr. Trump for his endorsement, Mr. Netanyahu said that Israel and the United States would never allow Iran to obtain nuclear weapons.

Mr. Hegseth also visited troops with U.S. Central Command, which overseas American military operations in the Middle East. On Tuesday, he posted photographs of himself speaking with soldiers in front of a fighter jet but did not say where the visit took place or whether he had traveled to Israel and met with Mr. Netanyahu.

Some American soldiers and refueling aircraft have been stationed in Israel since the United States and Israel started the war by attacking Iran in late February.

The U.S. military has prepared new strike plans for Iran, including sending more forces to the Middle East, even as Mr. Trump has been inconsistent in his public messaging about the war.

Some analysts say they believe that the United States will most likely decide to strike Iran in the coming weeks or months, given how far apart the Trump administration and Tehran are in negotiations.

“The base line expectation in Iran, and in Israel, is that it’s a matter of when the war restarts, not if,” said Raz Zimmt, director of the Iran program at the Institute for National Security Studies, a Tel Aviv-based research group.

“An airstrike alone will probably not achieve the goals the U.S. and Israel hope to complete — but it might give Trump an image of victory and a way out of the war,” Mr. Zimmt added.

The Israeli election will take place on Oct. 27. Polls suggest that Mr. Netanyahu is trailing Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff of the Israeli military under Mr. Netanyahu.

In a video statement on Tuesday, Mr. Netanyahu urged voters to support him, saying that he was the person Mr. Trump wanted by his side to “finish the job once and for all,” referring to the war on Iran.

Adam Rasgon contributed reporting to this article from Tel Aviv.

item.title: The Mayor Who Chose ‘to Stay and Fight’ as Gangs Laid Siege to His Town
item.description:
The mayor had a 9-millimeter handgun tucked in his waistband under his suit jacket. Police officers and civilians wearing balaclavas over their faces gathered outside the police station, gearing for battle.

Gangs seeking to control Kenscoff, his picturesque town in the hills above Haiti’s capital, had already attacked twice this summer, burning houses and killing people, he explained.

“The gangs want to kill me, too,” the mayor, Jean Massillon, told a team of visiting New York Times journalists in late September. “I have chosen to stay and fight.”

Police and government officials hadn’t listened when Mr. Massillon repeatedly told them that the gangs would attack, making him something of a Cassandra whose warnings went unheeded until many people were dead.

But Mr. Massillon, a longtime city administrator, refused to leave, even after other residents fled in August. He became the public face of the resistance against illegal armed groups wreaking havoc in his homeland.

He was also a symbol of how the Haitian state has effectively collapsed.

He suddenly fell ill on Oct. 9, while walking up a mountain on foot to reach an area the police had recently cleared of gangs. But the ambulance service had abandoned his city a year ago because of gang violence.

After six years serving as the appointed interim mayor of this town of about 50,000 people, Mr. Massillon died — another victim of Haiti’s yearslong decline and inability to protect its most vulnerable citizens. He was 53.

“There is a total decline of health care and security in Haiti; it’s like the country is dying,” Mr. Massillon’s brother, Christophe, said. “The whole of Haiti will remember that Jean stood up to defend the commune of Kenscoff and never gave up on this, even if he had to pay for it with his life.”

We met Mr. Massillon on the last Saturday in September, when we visited Kenscoff to report on a new United Nations-backed gang suppression force in Haiti.

Kenscoff had long been known as a peaceful mountainous farming village where Haiti’s elite went for weekend respites from the traffic-clogged capital, Port-au-Prince, a dozen miles away. But in recent years, Kenscoff had become a strategic point in Haiti’s battle against gangs that were increasingly making incursions into new territory.

It’s tactical because it borders Petion-Ville, a suburb where most diplomats and wealthy people live.

More than 22,000 people have been killed in gang violence in Haiti since 2021, and hundreds of them have died in Kenscoff.

“Twenty-one months we’ve been resisting and fighting,” the mayor said when we visited.

He showed us the bullet holes in the walls of City Hall.

The first attack, in January 2025, killed 139 people, according to the National Network for the Defense of Human Rights, a leading Haitian human rights organization.

Since then, Mr. Massillon sent at least 200 letters to police and government officials begging for help, the city manager, Emmanuel Pierre, said. He compiled them in a binder, which he was quick to show us.

Gang surveillance drones flew over his house. He fired off more letters.

“I can show you the papers that I wrote to the chief of the police to tell him that something has to be done, because we heard about something that is going to happen in the city,” Mr. Massillon told us.

His letter to the national police chief, Vladimir Paraison, was dated June 30. Between July 4 and 9, gangs arrived, killing 61 people, according to a United Nations panel of experts. The mayor put the body count at 105.

Despite the threats, the Haitian National Police withdrew key personnel and armored personnel carriers from the community, according to Kenscoff’s former police inspector and a report from a leading human rights group.

“We didn’t have any help,” Mr. Massillon said.

On Aug. 23 and 24, gangs conducted coordinated attacks on the city, killing 47 people, according to the mayor and the United Nations.

Yvener Metellus, a member of a local self-defense brigade, found his 79-year-old father burned alive in his home.

“I think the state is responsible,” he said, standing beside the home’s charred ruins.

The head of the National Police, Mr. Paraison, did not respond to repeated requests over several weeks for an interview. The police’s director of communications said he would refer a detailed list of questions to the agency’s high command.

The mayor also wrote Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé and the justice ministry. The prime minister’s office referred questions to the justice ministry, which did not respond to requests for comment.

Government officials in the capital had reached out to the local police inspector in charge of Kenscoff before the August massacre, and the commander claimed to have the situation under control, according to a senior Haitian official. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

The police response may have been complicated, the official said, by the fact that there were tensions between the mayor and the local police inspector, Nikenson Cadet.

Mr. Cadet has been removed from his post and is facing disciplinary hearings.

Mr. Cadet, in an interview, acknowledged that the police had withdrawn equipment and personnel before the latest massacre. But he said that, in his view, this indicated his superiors must have believed he was doing a good job and did not need additional resources.

He, too, had written to his superiors about the threats, but instead he became a scapegoat, he said.

“The problem is that we have a lack of human resources at the police department,” Mr. Cadet said. “We don’t have enough fire power to meet what the other guys have. We are overwhelmed by this situation.”

He said gangs had more machine guns than his officers did and that they had burned an armored personnel carrier.

In the hourslong telephone interview, which was conducted before Mr. Massilon died, Mr. Cadet also accused the mayor of complicity in the attacks. Mr. Massillon, he said, had suspiciously disarmed members of civilian self-defense groups just before the August killing spree.

Mr. Massillon’s brother called the accusation “absurd” and stressed that it was the job of the police, not the volunteer self-defense brigades, to protect the city.

A report by the National Network for the Defense of Human Rights said two members of the self-defense brigade had been disarmed after they committed an unlawful killing. The mayor “strongly denied” disarming them and stressed that he held no authority over them, the report said.

Marie Rosy Auguste Ducéna, who helped prepare the human rights group’s investigation, said the Haitian government was to blame for what happened in Kenscoff. Though the police inspector was the only person removed from his post, she confirmed that he had written at least two letters asking for ammunition, guns and armored vehicles.

“The first thing is the absence, not even the lack, but the absence, of will to protect the population,” she said. “They are never held accountable, really, in Haiti — never.”

Mr. Massillon died before The Times had the chance to ask about the police inspector’s accusations. His family and colleagues said the allegations had upset him, particularly after a political enemy denounced him on local radio.

Dr. Jean William Pape, a Weill Cornell Medical College professor who runs a clinic in Port-au-Prince and has a home in Kenscoff, spoke to the mayor the day before he died.

He said he had sounded tired and had not been taking medication for his high blood pressure.

“When politicians were lying about him on the radio station, he was profoundly hurt,” Dr. Pape said.

Dr. Pape’s home, just steps from the police station, was set ablaze during the August massacre. A security guard, a dozen horses and several dogs were killed.

Dr. Pape said he believes he was targeted because of his support for the mayor, who had spent the past year moving every few weeks to dodge gangs.

Mr. Massillon most likely died of heart failure or a stroke, Dr. Pape said. With the closest ambulance about 40 minutes away, his family drove him from one clinic to another, only to be told he had already died, Mr. Pierre, the city manager, said.

A month after the massacre, the Haitian National Police posted videos of the police and private military contractors taking back gang-occupied territory in Kenscoff. The U.N.’s gang suppression force never responded to Kenscoff, but took over positions in the capital previously manned by the Haitian National Police, enabling the police to deploy.

Townspeople in reclaimed areas are slowly returning, though people from other communities are still too afraid to go back. Several we spoke to had moved four times in two years, each time fleeing a massacre with just the clothes they had on.

Lerionne Louis, 63, is not even sure how many of her relatives died that August weekend. She saw about 23 cadavers.

Bodies are still missing.

“If there’s no security and no police presence,” Ms. Louis said, “that will take place again.”

Michael Anthony Adams and André Paultre contributed reporting.

item.title: Rubio Travels to India for Trade Talks Amid Strained U.S. Relations
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on Tuesday to boost trade ties and meet two of the country’s most powerful business leaders, even as attacks by President Trump have strained ties between the countries.

Mr. Rubio will meet with his Indian counterpart, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, as well as executives of half a dozen Indian companies that have a large presence in the United States. These include Asia’s two richest men, Gautam Adani and Mukesh Ambani.

Mumbai, India’s financial capital, was selected for the visit because of its intended focus on commercial diplomacy, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed members of the news media before Mr. Rubio’s trip. The official said the two countries were close to finalizing a bilateral trade deal, and that senior-level visits in both directions in recent months were focused on hammering out remaining details.

According to Randhir Jaiswal, the spokesman for India’s foreign ministry, the meeting will focus on “energy, trade, investment, defense, critical and emerging technologies.”

Mr. Adani, a billionaire who is a close ally of Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India, was indicted in the United States in 2024 on charges of bribery and fraud. But the criminal charges were dismissed in August, after Mr. Adani offered to invest billions of dollars in the United States. This spring, Mr. Trump announced that Mr. Ambani’s Reliance Industries would be a partner in building an oil refinery in Brownsville, Texas.

Mr. Rubio, who is widely seen as a contender in the next U.S. presidential election, is also expected to visit Jamnagar, a city in the state of Gujarat that houses the world’s largest oil refinery, which is owned by Reliance. In Jamnagar, Mr. Rubio is expected to stop in Vantara, a wildlife rescue center built by the Ambani family that has faced considerable criticism over its sourcing practices.

The ties between India and the United States have been rocky at best during the second Trump administration, in contrast to the warm relationship shared by Mr. Modi and Mr. Trump during the American president’s first term. The relationship has grown particularly frosty over the United States’ singling out India for its purchases of Russian oil, and it has been marked by a contrast between talks reflecting close ties and harsh attacks that have often caught Indian officials by surprise.

India has been facing threats of U.S. sanctions over its purchase of Russian oil. But the United States suddenly changed course earlier this month, announcing its own deal to purchase diesel from Russia.

Pragati K.B. and Edward Wong contributed reporting.
